slots.text: Once, when the price of spices in Holland had grown somewhat sluggish, the merchants had a few cargoes sunk in the sea to drive the price up. That was a pardonable, perhaps a necessary, deception. Is it something similar we need in the world of spirit? Are we so thoroughly convinced that we have arrived at the highest, that nothing is left for us but piously to persuade ourselves that we have not got so far — just to have something to fill the time with? Is it a self-deception of this kind that the present generation needs? Is it in virtuosity at this that it ought to be trained? Or is it not rather perfected enough already in the art of deceiving itself? Or is what it needs not rather an honest earnestness: one that fearlessly and incorruptibly points to the tasks; an honest earnestness that lovingly guards the tasks; one that does not frighten people into an anxious rush to take the highest by storm, but keeps the tasks young and beautiful, lovely to look at and beckoning to all, and yet at the same time difficult and inspiring to the noble — for the noble nature is inspired only by what is difficult? Whatever one generation may learn from another, what is truly human no generation learns from the one before it. In this respect every generation begins from the very beginning. It has no task other than that of every previous generation, and it gets no further either — provided the previous generation did not betray the task and deceive itself. This truly human thing is passion, in which one generation also fully understands the other, and understands itself. Thus no generation has learned to love from another; no generation gets to begin at any point other than the beginning; no later generation has a shorter task than the one before. And if, unlike the previous generations, one does not want to stop at loving here, but to go further, that is nothing but idle and foolish talk.

But the highest passion in a human being is faith, and here no generation begins at any point other than where the previous one began. Every generation begins all over again. The following generation gets no further than the previous one, provided that generation kept faith with its task and did not desert it. That this should be wearisome is, naturally, not something the generation can say; for it is the generation that has the task, and it has no concern with the fact that the previous generation had the same task — unless the individual generation, or the individuals in it, presumptuously want to take the place that belongs only to the spirit who governs the world and has the patience not to grow tired. If the generation starts on anything of that kind, it is topsy-turvy; and no wonder, then, if all of existence looks topsy-turvy to it. For surely no one has found existence more topsy-turvy than the tailor in the fairy tale who got up to heaven while still alive and looked at the world from that standpoint. As long as the generation concerns itself only with its task, which is the highest, it cannot grow tired; for the task is always enough for a human life. When children on a holiday have already played all their games before twelve o’clock, and now say impatiently, “Can’t anyone think up a new game?” — does that prove these children more developed and further along than those children, of their own or of a bygone generation, who could make the familiar games last all day? Or does it not rather prove that the first children lack what I would call the lovable earnestness that belongs to play?

Faith is the highest passion in a human being. In every generation there are perhaps many who do not even come to it, but no one gets further. Whether there are also many in our time who do not discover it, I do not decide. I dare appeal only to myself — to one who does not hide that he has a long way to go, though he does not on that account wish to deceive himself, or what is great, by turning it into a trifle, a childhood illness one must wish to get over as soon as possible. But even for the one who does not so much as come to faith, life has tasks enough; and if he loves them honestly, his life will not be wasted either, even if it is never like the lives of those who sensed and grasped the highest. But the one who has come to faith (whether he is exceptionally gifted or a simple soul makes no difference) does not stop at faith. Indeed, he would be offended if anyone said so to him, just as the lover would be indignant if people said that he stopped at love. For, he would answer, I am by no means standing still; my life is in it. Yet he does not get further either, not to anything else; for if he discovers that, then he has another explanation.

“One must go further; one must go further.” This urge to go further is old in the world. The obscure Heraclitus, who laid down his thoughts in his writings and laid down his writings in Diana’s temple (because his thoughts had been his armor in life, and so he hung it up in the temple of the deity), the obscure Heraclitus said: one cannot walk through the same river twice. The obscure Heraclitus had a disciple; he did not stop there, he went further and added: one cannot do it even once. Poor Heraclitus, to have a disciple like that! Through this improvement the Heraclitean thesis was improved into an Eleatic thesis that denies movement; and yet all that disciple wanted was to be a disciple of Heraclitus who went further — and not back to the position Heraclitus had abandoned.
